summary: Summation No. 15 covers December 1946 (with November production and trade statistics). Politically, the Diet's 91st extraordinary session passed the Cabinet Law, Imperial House Law, Imperial House Economy Law and House of Councillors Election Law, while the Social Democrats' 17 December dissolution resolution against the Yoshida Cabinet failed amid a 200,000-strong rally. The 21 December Nankai earthquake and tidal wave devastated Wakayama, Kochi and Shikoku. The Tokyo war crimes tribunal heard the B and C offenses, Japan-Netherlands and Philippines phases. Economically, coal output recovered, electric power was rationed, new coal prices and bonuses were set, Bank of Japan notes passed 93 billion yen, land reform machinery was created, and labor federations pressed for the cabinet's overthrow. Repatriation agreements with the Soviet Union were signed. A historian will find detailed production tables, union and dispute statistics, trade lists, and press comment.
highlights: On 17 December more than 200,000 workers rallied before the Imperial Palace against the Yoshida Cabinet, and the Social Democrats' resolution for Diet dissolution was defeated 160 against after five hours of debate, with 69 members abstaining.

The 91st extraordinary Diet (26 November-25 December) enacted the Cabinet Law, Imperial House Law, Imperial House Economy Law and a House of Councillors Election Law creating a 250-seat upper house (150 prefectural, 100 national); the Diet Law failed in the House of Peers.

The 21 December earthquake and tidal wave, centered off Wakayama, caused more than 3,500 casualties, destroyed thousands of homes and left over 90,000 homeless, with Shingu City nearly destroyed by fire.

On 24 December the Cabinet issued the ordinance implementing the Land Reform Law (transfer within two years) and created the Central Agricultural Land Commission; 9,851 village land commissions were elected by early returns.

SCAP and the Soviet representative signed a repatriation agreement on 19 December providing for return of Japanese at 50,000 per month and of Koreans in Japan to north of the 38th parallel; about 25,000 were already removed under the 26 November interim accord.

New coal prices took effect 1 November (consumer price 401.70 yen per ton, 168 percent higher) with output bonuses of 35-60 yen per ton; November coal output was 2,022,400 tons, 231,000 above October.

Bank of Japan notes in circulation reached 93,397,000,000 yen on 31 December, and the Diet passed supplemental budgets of 17,217,097,000 yen plus an Increased Income Tax Law expected to yield 4 billion yen.

Labor: 15,172 unions with 4,168,305 members were registered by 31 October; a 14 December ordinance dissolved the Tokyo Autonomous Labor Federation and barred wartime labor-front leaders; the electric-power dispute settled without a strike.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover, title page, table of contents for Parts I-IV, and the list of 101 charts, maps and graphs for Summation No. 15, December 1946.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Digest of the month: no change in SCAP organization, Diet and party politics, the earthquake, war crimes trials, production and labor, finance, repatriation, public health and press comment.

sections.title: Section 1. Organization under SCAP
sections.summary: Reports no change in the non-military organization of General Headquarters, SCAP, during December 1946.

sections.title: Section 2. Political Activities
sections.summary: The 91st Diet passed four implementing laws, and the 17 December dissolution resolution was defeated. Also covers the Korean illegal entry order, war crimes actions, crime, the 21 December earthquake and tribunal phases.

sections.title: Section 3. Economic Activities
sections.summary: Digest of crops, whaling, coal and oil output, textiles, the power shortage, the 14 December labor ordinance, trade, rice collections, 93.4 billion yen note circulation, holding companies and reparations.

sections.title: Section 4. Social Activities
sections.summary: Digest of 50 percent higher relief allowances, 25,000 Soviet-area repatriates, penicillin associations, falling dysentery, school lunches, women's meetings, radio series and press comment on the Yoshida Cabinet.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: The Diet's constitutional implementing laws, the opposition offensive against Yoshida, mass demonstrations and the Shikoku earthquake, and war crimes investigations and the international tribunal's three phases.

sections.title: Section 1. Government and Politics
sections.summary: The Diet passed the Cabinet, Imperial House, Imperial House Economy and Councillors Election laws; the Diet Law failed. The Social Democrats' dissolution resolution lost. Also Communist role, labor campaign and Education Ministry reorganization.

sections.title: The Diet
sections.summary: Four enacted laws, including the 250-member House of Councillors and Imperial Household property rules, and the Diet Law that failed over Article 84 joint conferences.

sections.title: Political Parties
sections.summary: Social Democratic left-right split over tactics; the 17 December dissolution resolution lost 160 against with 69 abstaining; government party reaction, coalition talk and Co-operative Democrat merger negotiations.

sections.title: Labor and Politics; Structural and Personnel Changes
sections.summary: Labor groups formed the National Movement for the Overthrow of the Cabinet on 24 December; the Education Ministry gained a Research Bureau; two advisory councils to the Finance Minister were created.

sections.title: Section 2. Public Safety
sections.summary: Mass demonstrations including 200,000 at the Palace on 17 December, black-market and poison-liquor arrests, police reforms, a record prison population of 70,753, fires, and the 21 December earthquake toll.

sections.title: Law and Order
sections.summary: Violence at the Tokyo Timepiece plant, a Korean demonstration at Yoshida's residence on 20 December, a sugar smuggling seizure, methyl-alcohol whiskey bootleggers and a narcotics ring broken.

sections.title: Police
sections.summary: 5 million yen for police communications, 600 prosecutors' assistants, year-end emergency police boxes, planned nationwide fingerprinting, October offenses down 9.5 percent, and juvenile crime incidents.

sections.title: Prisons
sections.summary: Prison officials' school to open 13 January, clothing shortage, November prison deaths of 144 versus 635 a year earlier, population of 70,753, and 3,449 juveniles in correction houses.

sections.title: Fire and Public Casualties
sections.summary: Shingu City burned after the quake, a Zushi repatriation center fire killed two, railway crowding casualties, 165 million yen of safety signs, a left-side traffic rule, and the earthquake damage table.

sections.title: Section 3. Legal and War Crimes
sections.summary: Illegal Korean entry order, provost court caseload of 1,315, atrocity investigations (1,105 cases on hand), Sugamo internments totaling 834, and tribunal testimony on POW camps, Java and the Philippines.

sections.title: Legal, Occupation Courts and War Crimes Investigation, Apprehension and Prosecution
sections.summary: 1,315 provost court cases; 12 names deleted and 28 released from Sugamo; two trials in Japan with three convictions including Tsuda's life sentence; Philippine detainee figures of 693.

sections.title: International Prosecution of War Criminals: First B and C Offenses Phase
sections.summary: Australian officers Coates and Blackburn testified on Burma-Siam railway camps, 55-Kilo camp ulcers and amputations, the Cycle Camp obedience form, and treatment in Formosa and Manchuria camps.

sections.title: International Prosecution of War Criminals: Japan-Netherlands Phase
sections.summary: Documents on Japanese demands on the Netherlands East Indies in 1940, a Balikpapan massacre affidavit, and De Weerd's testimony on the occupation of Java, Putera and the Soekarno independence committee.

sections.title: International Prosecution of War Criminals: Philippines B and C Offenses Phase
sections.summary: From 10 December: War Department casualty totals, testimony on the Bataan death march, Camp O'Donnell, Manila Hotel rapes, St. Paul's College and Lippa massacres, and US-Japan notes on prisoner treatment.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: Twelve sections on agriculture, mining, industry, textiles, utilities, labor, trade, rationing, finance and property control, mostly on November data: coal output 2,022,400 tons, 15,172 unions, notes at 93.4 billion yen.

sections.title: Section 1. Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: Rice estimate raised to 9,150,000 tons, record sweet potatoes, 24 December land reform ordinance with 9,851 land commissions elected, November fish catch 156,655 tons, Antarctic whaling, 151 steel fishing vessels authorized.

sections.title: Agriculture
sections.summary: Crop estimates, milk output at 30 percent of prewar average, feed imports down to 12,586 tons, a livestock census, and a Central Agricultural Land Commission of 23 commissioners.

sections.title: Fisheries
sections.summary: Fish landings, whaling fleets arriving 15 and 24 December, agar-agar and liver oil forecasts, fishing vessel construction, December petroleum allocations and extra rice rations for boat crews.

sections.title: Section 2. Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: November logs 415 million board feet, a charcoal rice incentive, coal output up to 2,022,400 tons, 1.9 billion yen coal rehabilitation loans, oil at 18,326 kiloliters, and October mineral gains.

sections.title: Forestry
sections.summary: Log production fell 32.8 million board feet, pulpwood rose 22 percent, charcoal reached 89,320 tons, firewood stayed well below plan, and full-time charcoal workers received added rice rations.

sections.title: Mining
sections.summary: Coal production, consumption and 887,000-ton stockpiles, lignite decline, power restored to mines, a petroleum quota of 226,320 kiloliters, drilling results and October metal output.

sections.title: Section 3. Heavy Industries
sections.summary: Coke 110,000 tons, aluminum 834 tons, copper and zinc output, rubber stocks down 24 percent, cement 63,885 tons, 20,995 buildings completed, ship repairs, chemical output at 34 percent of need.

sections.title: Coke and Metal Industries; Rubber and Petroleum
sections.summary: Coke allocations, iron and steel limited by coal, light metals, 3,725 tons blister copper, zinc and lead, 428 tons ferroalloys, rubber inventory and 828 kiloliters daily crude runs.

sections.title: Cement, Construction and Shipbuilding
sections.summary: Cement output, housing completions, a road budget of 834.7 million yen, 79.6 million yen of railway additions for Occupation Forces, repairs to 293 vessels and 151 new fishing vessels authorized.

sections.title: Chemical Industries and Machinery
sections.summary: Ammonium sulfate 46,700 tons, sulfuric acid at a postwar peak of 103,499 tons, salt output halved, machine tools up 13 percent, industrial machinery 278 million yen, textile machinery mostly repairs.

sections.title: Section 4. Manufacturing
sections.summary: Plan for 50 model rural factories, shrinking raw stocks in food processing, and output of pulp and paper, glass, optical goods, electrical equipment, truck chassis, bicycles, leather and farm implements.

sections.title: Section 5. Textile Industries
sections.summary: Cotton yarn up to 23,664,000 pounds, raw silk reeling 10,061 bales, rayon filament yarn below 1,000,000 pounds, wool gains, power cuts up to 50 percent, plus knit goods and dyeing.

sections.title: Cotton
sections.summary: Yarn production 88 percent of schedule, power cuts costing 1,000,000 pounds, cloth 44,038,000 square yards, and 649,858 bales of American cotton arrived.

sections.title: Silk
sections.summary: Raw silk 10,061 bales, 239 of 284 filatures operating, power use down 54 percent, cocoon stocks 148 million pounds, silk fabric 3,302,000 square yards.

sections.title: Rayon
sections.summary: Pulp receipts rose to 1,907 tons; filament yarn fell to 904,000 pounds, staple 1,689,000 pounds, spun yarn 735,000 pounds; Shikoku mills were short of coal and pulp.

sections.title: Wool, Hard and East Fibers, and Miscellaneous
sections.summary: Woolen yarn 2,062,000 pounds and worsted 842,000, flax and jute cut by power limits, throstle-spun yarn 534,000 pounds, and mixed fiber experiments.

sections.title: Knit Goods, Sewing Goods, Sundry Goods, Dyeing and Finishing
sections.summary: Knit underwear and gloves rose, deliveries doubled after the 1 November price rise, clothing stocks piled up in mills, thread output fell, and 23,750,102 square yards were dyed or finished.

sections.title: Section 6. Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: Coal shortage cut train-kilometers to 13.9 million and freight to 8,504,100 tons; hydro shortfall forced power limits up to 30 percent; 2,329,000,000 kilowatt hours generated; gas plants at 24.9 percent capacity.

sections.title: Section 7. Communications
sections.summary: Telephones reached 957,253, Tokyo-Osaka facsimile telegraph opened 22 December, Osaka phone rehabilitation finished, equipment output recovered after the Tokyo Shibaura strike, and broadcasting employed 7,018.

sections.title: Section 8. Labor
sections.summary: 14 December ordinance against wartime labor-front leaders, 15,172 unions, drive against the Yoshida Cabinet, Economic Reconstruction Conference, 1,501 collective agreements, winter allowances and lagging public works.

sections.title: Labor Legislation
sections.summary: The ordinance dissolving the Tokyo Autonomous Labor Federation affects over 10,000 persons; the Labor Standards Bill was deferred; unemployment and workmen's compensation insurance bills advanced.

sections.title: Labor and Employer Organizations
sections.summary: Union statistics by industry, 17 December joint demonstrations, Kyushu federation, coal miners' unification of 312,441 members, employer federations, and the 6 December Economic Reconstruction Conference.

sections.title: Labor Relations
sections.summary: Labor Relations Committees mediated electric-power and Tokyo Express disputes; 1,501 collective agreements; Tokyo metropolitan workers' contract for 51,000; Ordinance 591; 1,744,426 workers in disputes.

sections.title: Labor Education; Wages and Working Conditions
sections.summary: 36 pamphlets issued, labor schools held, family expenditure rising to 951.60 yen, Wage Investigation Commission approved 7 December, and a government winter allowance of two months' pay from 27 December.

sections.title: Public Works, Employment, Occupation Labor and Administration
sections.summary: Only 200,000 of 2,900,000 scheduled public works jobs were filled, 9,639 were in vocational training, 180,000 daily Occupation workers were paid 1.126 billion yen, and former police were excluded from labor posts.

sections.title: Section 9. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: New Boeki Cho branches, 150,000,000 square yards of textiles allocated to Asian colonies, first raw fur shipment to the US, 400,000 tons of Red Sea salt, tea and equipment shipments to Korea and China.

sections.title: Section 10. Rationing and Price Control
sections.summary: 52.1 days of staple food held, rice collections at 36.7 percent of quota, 2 December food price increases, new coal price of 401.70 yen, 993,800 barrels of US petroleum, 89,524 violations.

sections.title: Section 11. Finance
sections.summary: Foreign currency surrender to the Bank of Japan, notes at 93,397,000,000 yen, 17.2 billion yen supplemental budget, 9.3 billion yen bond issue, 240 billion yen national debt, Bank of Tokyo inaugural meeting 16 December.

sections.title: Money and Banking
sections.summary: Foreign exchange surrender order of 29 November, Bank of Japan statement totaling 96,446 million yen, bank new and old accounts, postal savings of 50,262 million yen in 199 million accounts.

sections.title: Liquidation
sections.summary: Five Nanyo Colonization and Manchuria subsidiaries were closed in November and added to the institutions under the Committee of Conservators for Closed Institutions.

sections.title: Public Finance
sections.summary: Increased Income Tax Law for 4 billion yen, three supplemental budgets, special accounts, 150 billion yen domestic bonds, a 90 million yen farm settler fund, and Old Court Nobles Fund distribution.

sections.title: Section 12. Property Control and Reparations
sections.summary: War-criminal suspects' property of 69.5 million yen, wartime patent dispositions, precious metals allocations, repatriates' seized currency, 20 holding companies designated 3 December, and reparations catalogs.

sections.title: Property Control
sections.summary: 721 suspects' inventories, 3,066 UN patents registered at 7 December 1941, release of gold and silver, SCAP custody accounts, and about 5,037,000 repatriates processed.

sections.title: Antitrust and Cartels
sections.summary: Japan Precision Industry put under surveillance, 20 Mitsui, Mitsubishi and other firms designated for liquidation, Dental Materials Control Company dissolved, Economic Stabilization Board Regulations 2 to 4.

sections.title: Reparations
sections.summary: Conversion permits limited to reparations plants, a catalog of 25,000 machine tools, 12 thermal plants listed, only 30 percent of aluminum plant equipment removable, and a new Reparations Division.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Public health, welfare and repatriation, communicable disease and vital statistics, then education, school lunches, information programs, radio, press comment, films and the library.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: 2,658,769 relief recipients, 50 percent higher cash allowances, quake relief, the 19 December Soviet repatriation agreement, penicillin production, dysentery down to 73.4, and November births of 195,993.

sections.title: Public Welfare and Repatriation
sections.summary: Relief grants of 115 million yen, US relief supplies, earthquake aid, 98,022 repatriated in December, and the 19 December agreement for 50,000 a month from Soviet areas.

sections.title: Hospitals, Veterinary, Dental and Nursing Affairs
sections.summary: 3,900 hospitals with 218,014 beds, 262 doctors licensed, milk and meat inspection faults, animal disease counts, and a nursing school recognized as a college.

sections.title: Supply
sections.summary: Penicillin associations and 22 producing plants, medicine production of 194 million yen, vaccine figures, hydrogen cyanide fumigation, and narcotics convictions including a naval officer's three-year sentence.

sections.title: Preventive Medicine, Nutrition and Vital Statistics
sections.summary: Typhus 2.1, diphtheria 78.6, dysentery 73.4 per 100,000; eleven quarantine ports declared; November births 195,993 and deaths 88,425; explanation of the September marriage spike.

sections.title: Section 2. Education and Media of Expression
sections.summary: Social Education News launched 12 December, 6,164 usable school projectors, school lunch program, 1,601,781 yen from banned textbooks, women's meetings, radio series, press comment, films with 870,516 attendance.

sections.title: Education and Arts
sections.summary: Hiroshima social education progress, a visual education survey, a vocational guidance exhibit, school lunches in Chiba, banned textbook disposal, and the Osaka-Kobe art society.

sections.title: Media of Expression
sections.summary: Women's organizations, 'Information Please' broke records with 17,000 letters, Tokyo and prefectural press on the Yoshida Cabinet and reparations, educational film attendance and the library; page 134 is a map of Japan.
